items.summary: People love to argue about whether AIs could recursively self-improve their way to superintelligence, each improvement making the next one easier as progress accelerates. I'm unsure. It could be that progress stalls at near-human or somewhat superhuman levels, that the ultimate qualitative limits of intelligence are not particularly beyond the human-level, or that the quantity of AI researchers involved is so vast that substantially superhuman AIs are created without strictly entering a super-exponential regime. But honestly, I think recursive self-improvement is a little overrated. Even if human-level AIs do not rapidly lead to superhuman AIs, the vast quantities of them could be very dangerous. Arguments against recursive self-improvement provide little consolation here. Conversely, recursive self-improvement to superintelligence does…

items.summary: arXiv:2610.35193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems built around large models increasingly use experience and feedback to make persistent changes to models, prompts, memories, tools, and workflows. items.summary: arXiv:2610.35434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. We present Skill$^{\infty}$, which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. items.summary: arXiv:2610.35766v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-supervised training is monitored without labels, through the loss and statistics of the learned features. We report a case where we know the encoders lost part of what they had learned, so we can check whether these signals noticed. We trained LeJEPA encoders on synthetic images with known generating factors. In nine of ten seeds, the readability of those factors fell abruptly and stayed down, nearly always along the same direction in factor space. Meanwhile the loss kept falling, and most of the eleven label-free signals we tracked kept improving and rated the declining runs better than runs that did not decline. Standard change-point detection rarely flagged the decline near its onset, and selecting checkpoints by these signals mostly chose ones after it.
items.title: Improving Signals, Declining Encoder: A Known-Answer Test of Label-Free Monitoring in Self-Supervised Learning

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based personal agents are increasingly deployed to handle everyday tasks on users' behalf. items.summary: Evolution strategies (ES) update a model by sampling a population of perturbed copies, scoring each one, and moving in the reward-weighted direction of the perturbations. Once rewards are assigned, it balances at its reward-weighted center of mass instead. items.summary: Let $X_2$ be a complex primitive double scheme, $X=(X_2)_{red}$. The ideal sheaf of $X$ is a line bundle on $X$. Let $E$ be a coherent sheaf on $X_2$. Then there exists a nonempty open subset $U$ of $X_2$ and integers $m_1$, $m_2$, uniquely determined by $E$, such that $E_{|U}$ is locally isomorphic to $(O_X\otimes C^{m_1})\oplus(O_{X_2}\otimes C^{m_2})$. If we can take $U=X_2$, we say the $E$ is quasi locally free. If $m_1=1$ we say that $E$ is rigid. In this case, we show that deformations of $E$ are of the same type. So locally free sheaves and rigid quasi locally free sheaves on $X_2$ play the same role on $X_2$ as locally free sheaves do on smooth schemes. In this paper we study the existence and description of quasi locally free sheaves, and flat families of such sheaves.
items.title: Quasi locally free sheaves on primitive double schemes

items.summary: In this paper, we prove a sharp effective Nullstellensatz for projective Cohen-Macaulay schemes of pure dimension over an arbitrary field. In particular, if L is an ample line bundle on a smooth complex projective variety X and J is a coherent ideal sheaf with J\otimes L globally generated, then (\sqrt{J})^{°_L X}\subseteq J. This establishes the sharp bound conjectured by Ein and Lazarsfeld. More generally, we obtain sharp bounds in terms of mixed intersection numbers and a refinement involving products of powers of prime ideal sheaves associated to the irreducible components of the base locus. We also establish sharp radical power bounds for homogeneous ideals in finitely generated standard graded Cohen-Macaulay domains, extending Kollár's sharp effective Nullstellensatz for polynomial rings. items.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language models. Most critically, we find that important layers are highly task-dependent, with limited overlap across tasks. Motivated by these insights, we propose Adaptive-LoRA, a calibration-driven method that automatically identifies task-specific layers via frozen-base zero-ablation, enabling efficient layer selection without exhaustive search. items.summary: As AI agents become more capable, and as individuals, companies, institutions, and governments come to rely on them for an ever wider range of tasks, the question of whether these agents can be trusted will become increasingly important. There are two distinct components of agent trustworthiness that are useful to distinguish. The first, which we label loyalty, concerns whether an agent is genuinely attempting to carry out the user's instructions and act in accordance with their interests. The second, which we label reliability, concerns whether an agent is capable enough to accomplish the tasks that we assign to it. An example of the latter failure (unreliability) would be an agent tasked with maintaining an application accidentally deleting a critical database. items.summary: Let $G$ and $H$ be Gram matrices of spherical $2$-designs on the same number of indices. We study when their Schur product is again the Gram matrix of a spherical design. We give a criterion in terms of orthogonal projections with constant diagonal, and an explicit $15$-point spherical $3$-design whose Gram matrix belongs to no symmetric Bose-Mesner algebra. For a symmetric association scheme, the factorization problem takes the form $v(E_S\circ E_T)=μE_U$. This is a counterpart of ordinary matrix product factorizations in the adjacency basis. The case $E_U=I-E_0$ gives a dual near-factorization and has a regular simplex as its normalized output. We characterize complementary input supports by a strongly regular fusion, give a reciprocal criterion, and classify the case in which one factor is the last Hamming idempotent.
items.title: Dual near-factorizations and Schur products in association schemes

items.summary: I am often skeptical of arguments about China that rely heavily on personal experience. The author may explicitly acknowledge that their experience is limited without appropriately treating their arguments with rigor beforehand. This acknowledgment may thus sit beside conclusions about the values, behaviors, and functions of Chinese society without meaningfully constraining any of them. Different speakers may each have peers with similar experiences that corroborate their claims, or repeated experiences that solidify their firsthand evidence. We may believe one or another speaker is more perceptive, well-informed, or more willing to acknowledge facts contrary to their beliefs. However, the critical question is how far these accounts support the conclusions being drawn. I will address here how we should evaluate firsthand accounts…

items.summary: Best-of-N (BoN) inference returns the candidate with the highest proxy reward, so a larger $N$ tests the proxy's extreme tail more than its average ranking quality. We show that the exact BoN value is a Beta-weighted integral of conditional true reward over within-prompt score quantiles. It follows that BoN depends on scores only through their ranks. It also follows that BoN can decline only if the calibration curve in the tail turns downward, and the budget where the decline appears depends on where that turn lies. Under a bounded additive model, the error tail sets the limit: Gaussian errors keep improving, Laplace errors reach a plateau, and heavy-tailed errors return to the prior mean. When error variance is largest at low true reward, even Gaussian noise can push BoN below random selection. Synthetic phase maps agree with this…

items.summary: Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. items.summary: For any fixed number $k\ge3$ of independent volume-sampled sites in the unit-area Brownian map, we represent the negative-power transform of their ordinary Voronoi volumes as a finite sum of marked planar scheme integrals. These integrals arise from the critical asymptotics of generating functions for face-constrained labelled planar maps. To connect them to Voronoi volumes, we use Miermont's zero-delay correspondence to interpret the labelled maps as quadrangulations with distinguished sites and then pass to the Brownian map scaling limit.

items.summary: Book Review: The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence, by Kevin Roose. This is a story of AI as seen through the eyes of the people who are creating it. My first impression of Roose was of his famous conversation with Sydney. I guessed that he got Sydney to say outrageous things because he wanted a sensational story. But I kept hearing occasional hints, from people who took AI seriously, that Roose was more responsible than that. So I reluctantly bought the book. The hints were correct. The full story behind that conversation seems better described as “‘freeing the Shoggoth‘, enabled by some Microsoft mistakes”. I’m unsure how deeply Roose understands AI, but he at least is pretty competent at getting an AI to correct any mistakes about AI that he was tempted to make. Underestimating AI…

items.summary: How does pre-trained model capacity relate to performance after adaptation for causal tasks? We study two systems built on the Qwen 2.5 family: CausalLLM, which estimates scalar potential outcomes with treatment-specific heads, and CausalGen, which generates treatment-conditioned text or code using soft prefixes and factual supervised fine-tuning (SFT), counterfactual SFT, and preference alignment. Increasing backbone size from 0.5B to 1.5B yields mixed scalar-estimation results on IHDP, but improves CodeGen pass@1 from 0.267 to 0.575 and treatment-effect score from 0.231 to 0.515 after the complete generative pipeline. Within 0.5B CausalLLM, narrative inputs reduce mean sqrt(PEHE) from 1.842 to 1.780, a 3.4% improvement over tabular inputs; the 5.8% improvement over a no-LLM baseline combines changes in representation and input format…
items.title: When Does Pre-Trained Capacity Help Causal Learning? From Scalar Prediction to Counterfactual Post-Training

items.summary: Last week at a small conference, there was talk about a future event referred to as The Hackening. As in, within 6-12 months, many predicted that due to advanced AIs and AI agents the internet would become a severely hostile place. Some worried that this could rise to the level of ‘assume any phone connected to the internet is rooted’ and several people urged doing general crisis preparations on a personal level, in case of disruptions in supply lines, power, water or internet. It did not take long for things to escalate. The biggest hack is a flaw in PHP, which can be exploited to take control of the computer running any website suing an unpatched version of PHP. There are many others. On a personal level, you want to do at least some basic prep and get your security in order. It is cheap to do as a form of insurance, and being caught…

items.summary: TLDR: I lightly extend Ward, Hu et al (2026) to measure how well gradient routing generalizes. I route gradients on one type of reward hack (e.g. ones that reason in English) and check whether this suppresses other types at test time (e.g. ones that reason in French), despite the model being trained on those too. This models a realistic monitor that catches some types of hack during training but not others, rather than catching each at the same rate. I find encouraging evidence of generalization, as well as some failures I don’t yet understand. Introduction Recently, Ward, Hu et al (2026) used gradient routing to prevent reward hacking learnt during training from showing up at test time. I think their method is pretty promising. items.summary: Cybersecurity operators increasingly encounter sophisticated and fast-paced attacks, making autonomous cyber defense (ACD) a critical approach for supporting timely and effective decision-making. Reinforcement learning (RL)-based ACD agents have the ability to autonomously observe network states and take actions to defend and recover system assets, making them well suited for ACD. However, these agents often face critical trade-offs, such as improving network security while inadvertently degrading service availability or violating other operational priorities such as confidentiality and integrity, raising the core challenge of aligning agent behavior with human-specified goals and intent. In this work, we study the problem of aligning RL-based ACD agents with human-specified operational objectives without requiring costly retraining. We…
items.title: Alignment of Autonomous Cyber Defense Agents via Adaptive Policy Shaping

items.summary: Alignment evaluations aim to assess whether large language models would engage in dangerous misaligned behaviour. Misaligned and evaluation-aware models might engage in alignment faking, where they pursue a hidden goal, but conceal this behaviour when they suspect effective oversight such as during training, evaluation or audited deployment. Such a model might view any prompt-based intervention that aims to reveal latent propensities as part of the evaluation, calling into question the reliability of existing alignment evaluations. Current methods for detecting alignment faking rely on chain-of-thought monitorability, highly realistic environments that reduce evaluation awareness, or mechanistic interventions, all of which are expected to become less reliable for future model generations. We present a method for revealing latent…
items.title: Propensities Please: Exposing Alignment-Faking LLMs using Synthetic Document Finetuning

items.summary: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also…
items.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning

items.summary: Whether AI systems could take power from humans matters a great deal for how much risk we face from them. Answering that requires a correct picture of how power works, which is what this guide tries to give. In short, power rests on self-reinforcing expectations. A ruler has power if everyone expects everyone else to enforce their commands, even if this is bad for almost everyone involved. But expectations can also shift suddenly, and when they do, change is rapid and chaotic. This can sometimes allow small, coordinated groups to seize control over much larger societies. Almost any rule can enforce itself Consider the classic tragedy of the commons. A village has a common green where everyone can graze their cows. Each villager gains from grazing as much as they can, but if everyone does, the grass dies and the green becomes useless…
items.title: Power — a guide for the perplexed

items.summary: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new…
items.title: Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation

items.summary: Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b…
items.title: Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery

items.summary: We have a tendency to judge past societies more harshly than our own. That is partly because we tend to focus on the evils of past societies that many people at the time either weren’t aware of, or didn’t spend much time thinking about. Most Germans claimed to be unaware of the extent of Nazi war crimes until they were revealed after the war ended. Few Britons were aware of the brutality of the slave trade until Thomas Clarkson’s anti slavery investigations of the 18th century. During the colonial period, most Europeans were unaware of the extent of the abuses inflicted on indigenous people. Few people were aware of the abuses that took place in large scale psychiatric institutions in the 1950s. Some people argue that our current society will be judged harshly by future generations for the way it treats factory farmed animals - which is…
items.title: The Evil is where you aren’t looking

items.summary: One hot topic of conversation right now is “What are all the humans going to do when AI plus humanoid robotics becomes better at everything?”. As William Gibson famously said “The future is already here — it’s just not very evenly distributed”. So it’s worth looking at what activities are already taking up excess human time, allowing humans to form status hierarchies, and satisfying the human need to feel like they are accomplishing something. One of those activities is video games, which continue to take up an increasing fraction of people’s time. But many other human activities can in some senses be seen as being forms of gaming - in the sense that they are activities that lead to dubious material benefits, but allow people to gain status and feel accomplished. This includes a large fraction of academia (definitely not all), the art…
items.title: Is Gaming the Future of Humanity?

items.summary: A linear monodimensional lattice Boltzmann scheme with three velocities tackling the advection equation is investigated. We prove that it is second-order accurate and provide necessary and sufficient stability conditions through an explicit formula involving the two relaxation parameters. Relying on existing results for finite difference schemes, we prove convergence for smooth initial data with initialization of the non-conserved moments at equilibrium. Several numerical simulations illustrate these theoretical findings.
items.title: Numerical analysis of a Lax-Wendroff type lattice Boltzmann scheme for the advection equation
